title: Sandbox activities: claim, run, park, release

story: The run for RH-1234 asks for a lite VM. The orchestrator, the Temporal worker that does the outside work of every run, finds a warm one, detaches it from its pool and tags it as this run's. One second later, before it can report back, its pod is restarted during a routine deploy.

Temporal, the workflow engine that records every step of the run, sees that the step never finished, so after a short wait it runs the same step again on another worker. That is exactly what Temporal is for. But the step is "take a VM from the pool", and if it simply runs again, it takes a second VM. The first one is now tagged for a run that will never use it, and it costs money until something notices.
hook.question: How do we write the steps that claim, run and release a VM, so that running any of them twice does no harm?

read.h: Temporal will run your step again
p: In Temporal, the steps that touch the outside world are activities: plain async functions that the workflow calls, and that may use the AWS SDK, the network and the clock. The life of a sandbox VM is a handful of them. acquireSandbox takes a VM of the right size from its warm pool. freshenSandbox brings it to the run's commit. workInSandbox starts the harness, our program that runs the Claude session on the VM, and follows it. parkSandbox stops a VM that is waiting for a person, and wakeSandbox starts it again. releaseSandbox ends it.

Temporal records each activity's result once it finishes. If a worker dies first, Temporal cannot know how far the function got, so it retries the activity from the start. The side effect may already have happened: the VM detached, the harness started, the instance terminated. So the rule for every one of these activities is the same: it must be idempotent, which means that running it twice has the same effect as running it once.

read.h: Claim: look for your own VM first
p: The claim makes itself safe to repeat with one question at the start: is there already a VM tagged with this run's ID? If there is, a previous attempt got that far, and the activity returns that VM instead of taking another. Only if there is none does it raise the group's desired capacity by one, wait for a new VM to be in service, detach it so the group forgets it, and tag it with the run ID, the agent, the ticket and a lease, the time until which the run promises to look after it.

Two runs can also reach for the same new VM at the same moment. Detaching is the referee: AWS lets only one detach succeed, so the loser's call fails, and it moves on to the next VM. The lab shows the first case with real AWS calls against LocalStack, a program that answers AWS API calls on your laptop.

notes.text: The idempotency check. A retry after a crash finds the VM the first attempt already took.
Waiting for a VM can take a minute; the heartbeat tells Temporal this worker is still alive.
Detach with "decrement desired capacity": the group forgets the VM, and Temporal owns it from here.
Another claim won this VM. Try the next one.
Run ID, agent, ticket and a lease of two hours, renewed while the run lives.

read.see:
$ CRASH=1 ./acquire.sh run-7f3a
worker died after tagging i-52b9d909d01556c40
$ ./acquire.sh run-7f3a        # Temporal's retry
already claimed for run-7f3a: i-52b9d909d01556c40

p: workInSandbox has the same problem in another form. It starts the harness over SSM, AWS's way of sending a command to a machine that accepts no connections, as a systemd unit named after the run, because a run can last longer than any SSM command may. Then it follows the run: every 30 seconds it reads the harness's last heartbeat from the broker, the service that holds our keys and also receives those heartbeats, reports its own heartbeat to Temporal, and renews the VM's lease every five minutes. It returns when the harness says done, needs an answer, preempted or failed.

A retry of workInSandbox must not start a second harness on the same VM. So it first asks systemd whether the run's unit is already active, and only starts it if not; otherwise it simply begins following again. The harness never noticed that the worker watching it was replaced. If the harness itself goes silent for five minutes, the activity fails with SandboxDead, a failure Temporal does not retry, because the workflow must decide what happens next.

deeper.h: Go deeper: park, wake and retire
p: A VM that waits for a person should not cost 42 cents an hour. After 10 idle minutes the workflow calls parkSandbox: stop the instance, keep its disk, and set the lease to 73 hours from now. wakeSandbox starts it again when the answer comes, waits about a minute for SSM to be online and freshens it if main moved. After 72 hours stopped, retireSandbox starts it once more, pushes a final checkpoint and terminates it; the next answer continues on a fresh VM. Each of these is safe to repeat too: stopping a stopped VM or tagging a tagged one changes nothing.

On a Spot VM, a small timer on the machine writes a file when AWS announces it will take the machine back. The harness checkpoints and exits as preempted, and the workflow retries the step on a fresh VM from the same group.

releaseSandbox runs in the workflow's finally block, so it runs however the run ends: done, failed, stopped by a person or cancelled. It revokes the run's scope in the broker, so the capability on the VM stops working everywhere, then terminates the instance. Both calls are already idempotent except for one answer: when the VM no longer exists, AWS says InvalidInstanceID.NotFound. For a release that is exactly the state we wanted, so the activity treats that one error as success and throws every other error again.

notes.text: Revoke first: deleting a scope that is already gone is fine too.
Gone is what we wanted. Anything else, such as a missing permission, must still fail loudly.

$ ./release.sh i-52b9d909d01556c40
i-52b9d909d01556c40 -> shutting-down
$ ./release.sh i-0000000000000dead
i-0000000000000dead is already gone: nothing to do

lab.title: A claim that survives a crash
needs: AWS CLI v2 and the LocalStack image from the p3-1 lab (localstack/localstack:4.9)
No AWS account: every call goes to LocalStack on your laptop
lab.goal: Claim a warm VM in a way that a retry after a crash returns the same VM, show what a claim without that check does, and release a VM twice without an error.

guess.q: The claim tags a VM with run-7f3a and then the worker dies before it returns. Temporal runs the claim again. With no check at the start, what happens?

options.text: Temporal remembers the VM from the first attempt and passes it in.
options.why: Temporal only records results of activities that finished. The first attempt never returned, so Temporal knows nothing about the VM.

options.text: The retry takes a second VM, and the first one stays tagged for a run that will never use it.
options.why: Without looking for its own VM first, the retry cannot know the first attempt got that far.

options.text: AWS refuses to tag a second VM with the same run ID.
options.why: Tags are not unique in AWS. Any number of machines can carry the same tag.

follow.say: Start LocalStack and point the AWS CLI at it in this terminal, then create two warm lite VMs.
follow.do:
docker run --rm -d --name localstack -p 4566:4566 localstack/localstack:4.9 && sleep 15
export AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=test AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=test AWS_DEFAULT_REGION=us-east-1 AWS_ENDPOINT_URL=http://localhost:4566
aws ec2 run-instances --image-id ami-ff0fea8310f3 --count 2 --instance-type m8i.xlarge \
  --tag-specifications 'ResourceType=instance,Tags=[{Key=ai-agents:managed,Value=true},{Key=ai-agents:pool,Value=lite}]' \
  --query 'Instances[].InstanceId' --output text

follow.say: Save the claim and the release. The claim looks for its own VM first; CRASH=1 makes it die right after tagging, like the pod in the story.
follow.do:
mkdir -p ~/academy-labs/g3-8 && cd ~/academy-labs/g3-8
cat > acquire.sh <<'EOF'
#!/bin/sh
# acquire.sh <run-id>: claim one warm lite VM for this run. Safe to run again after a crash.
run=$1
mine=$(aws ec2 describe-instances --output text --query 'Reservations[].Instances[].InstanceId' \
  --filters Name=tag:ai-agents:run-id,Values=$run Name=instance-state-name,Values=pending,running,stopped)
if [ -n "$mine" ]; then echo "already claimed for $run: $mine"; exit 0; fi

vm=$(aws ec2 describe-instances --output text \
  --query 'Reservations[].Instances[] | [?!(Tags[?Key==`ai-agents:run-id`])].InstanceId | [0]' \
  --filters Name=tag:ai-agents:pool,Values=lite Name=instance-state-name,Values=running)
if [ "$vm" = "None" ]; then echo "no warm lite VM left: a cold start"; exit 1; fi
aws ec2 create-tags --resources $vm --tags Key=ai-agents:run-id,Value=$run
[ "$CRASH" = 1 ] && { echo "worker died after tagging $vm"; exit 1; }
echo "claimed $vm for $run"
EOF
cat > release.sh <<'EOF'
#!/bin/sh
# release.sh <instance-id>: called from the workflow's finally. A VM that is already gone is fine.
out=$(aws ec2 terminate-instances --instance-ids "$1" --query 'TerminatingInstances[0].CurrentState.Name' --output text 2>&1)
case "$out" in
  *InvalidInstanceID.NotFound*) echo "$1 is already gone: nothing to do" ;;
  *error*|*Error*) echo "$out" >&2; exit 1 ;;
  *) echo "$1 -> $out" ;;
esac
EOF
chmod +x acquire.sh release.sh

lab.build: Make the claim respect the size. Give the warm VMs a second tag, ai-agents:size (lite or full), create one full VM next to the lite ones, and change acquire.sh to take the size as a second argument: ./acquire.sh run-7f3a full. The "already claimed" check must also confirm that the VM it found has the size that was asked for, and say so if it does not, because a retry must return the same kind of VM the run asked for.
lab.fix: A teammate removed the three lines at the top of acquire.sh because "the lookup costs one extra API call on every claim". Recreate it with sed '4,6d' acquire.sh > naive.sh, create two fresh warm VMs, run CRASH=1 ./naive.sh run-x and then ./naive.sh run-x. List the VMs tagged run-x: there are two. Explain what each one costs until something finds it, which job finally removes the orphan and when, and why one API call is the cheaper price.
checks: After the crash, the retry prints "already claimed" with the same instance ID.
The third claim finds no warm VM and reports a cold start instead of taking a VM that belongs to another run.
Releasing the same VM twice succeeds both times, and releasing an unknown ID says "already gone".
Without the check (naive.sh), the crash and retry leave two VMs tagged with the same run.
You stopped LocalStack: docker stop localstack.

solution.text:
run=$1; size=$2
mine=$(aws ec2 describe-instances --output text \
  --query 'Reservations[].Instances[].[InstanceId, Tags[?Key==`ai-agents:size`].Value | [0]]' \
  --filters Name=tag:ai-agents:run-id,Values=$run Name=instance-state-name,Values=pending,running,stopped)
if [ -n "$mine" ]; then
  set -- $mine
  [ "$2" = "$size" ] || { echo "run $run already holds $1, but it is $2, not $size"; exit 1; }
  echo "already claimed for $run: $1"; exit 0
fi
vm=$(aws ec2 describe-instances --output text \
  --query 'Reservations[].Instances[] | [?!(Tags[?Key==`ai-agents:run-id`])].InstanceId | [0]' \
  --filters Name=tag:ai-agents:pool,Values=$size Name=tag:ai-agents:size,Values=$size Name=instance-state-name,Values=running)
# ...the rest as before

explain: Why can Temporal not simply remember which VM the first attempt took?
How does workInSandbox avoid starting a second harness when it is retried?
Why does releaseSandbox treat InvalidInstanceID.NotFound as success, but no other error?
lab.done: A crashed claim's retry returns the same VM, a full pool gives a cold start instead of stealing, and a release can run any number of times.

check.q: acquireSandbox detached and tagged a VM, then its worker died. Temporal retries the activity. What makes the retry return the same VM?

options.text: It first looks for a VM already tagged with this run's ID and returns it
options.why: The tag is written in AWS, so it survives the worker. That one lookup turns a retry into a no-op.

options.text: Temporal passes the first attempt's result to the retry
options.why: The first attempt never returned, so there is no result to pass.

options.text: The warm pool gives back the same VM to the same caller
options.why: The VM was already detached from the pool, which no longer knows about it.

check.q: workInSandbox is retried on a new worker while the harness is still working on the VM. What should the retry do?

options.text: Start the harness again, to be sure it is running
options.why: Two harnesses on one VM would work on the same branch and session at once.

options.text: See that the run's systemd unit is active and start following its heartbeats again
options.why: The harness does not depend on the worker that watches it, so a new worker just re-attaches.

options.text: Throw SandboxDead, because the old worker is gone
options.why: SandboxDead means the harness went silent, not the worker. Here the harness is fine.

check.q: releaseSandbox calls terminate on a VM, and AWS answers InvalidInstanceID.NotFound. What should happen?

options.text: The activity fails, so a person checks what happened
options.why: A missing VM is the goal of a release. Failing would make every retried finally block noisy for nothing.

options.text: The activity retries until AWS finds the VM
options.why: It will never be found; it is gone, which is what we wanted.

options.text: The activity treats it as success, but still throws any other error
options.why: Gone is the desired state. Other errors, such as a missing permission, mean the VM may still be running.

p: The activities live in ai-agents/orchestrator/src/activities/sandbox.ts and run.ts, as plain async functions on AWS SDK v3, unit-tested with aws-sdk-client-mock. acquireSandbox({ size, runId, agent, jiraKey, spot }) raises desired capacity on ai-agents-sandbox-<size> or its -spot group, detaches with ShouldDecrementDesiredCapacity, tags ai-agents:run-id, agent, jira and lease-until, counts cold starts as a metric, opens the broker scope, mints the gateway run token and writes the task, capability and token to /run/nova/ over SSM (mode 0600, owner agent). freshenSandbox fetches the commit through the broker, reinstalls only lockfiles that differ from the image manifest, refreshes FCP Lab on full and wide, and throws LabNotReady when the lab will not start. ticketToPr claims lite for the plan and full for the build.

workInSandbox starts the harness with systemd-run --uid agent --unit nova-<run> over SSM if it is not running, reads heartbeats from the broker's internal API every 30 s, heartbeats to Temporal, renews the lease every 5 minutes, and throws a non-retryable SandboxDead after 5 minutes of silence. parkSandbox, wakeSandbox and retireSandbox handle waits (10 idle minutes, lease now + 73 h, retire after 72 h); releaseSandbox revokes the scope and terminates in the workflow's finally. routineRun reuses the same activities.

tickets.why: acquireSandbox and freshenSandbox: claim the right size, detach, tag, open the scope, write the run's files, freshen only the delta.
workInSandbox, park, wake, retire and release, each safe to retry.

words.plain: A step of a Temporal workflow that touches the outside world, such as an AWS call. Temporal retries it if its worker dies.
Safe to run twice: the second run has the same effect as the first, so a retry does no harm.
Take a VM out of its Auto Scaling group, so the group forgets it and Temporal owns it.
A retried activity finds the work already running and follows it, instead of starting it again.
A claim that finds no warm VM and must wait for a new one to be built and set up.

review.q: For acquireSandbox, workInSandbox and releaseSandbox, say what each one checks or tolerates so that a retry is harmless.
review.a: acquire: looks for a VM tagged with this run ID first. workInSandbox: starts the harness's systemd unit only if it is not already active, otherwise re-attaches. release: revoking a missing scope and InvalidInstanceID.NotFound both count as success.

review.q: Two claims race for the same new VM. What decides the winner, and what does the loser do?
review.a: The detach call: AWS lets only one succeed. The loser's detach throws, it skips that VM and takes the next new one in service.

remember: Temporal will run a step again after a crash, so every step that touches a VM first checks what an earlier attempt already did: find your own VM, re-attach to your own harness, and treat "already gone" as done.
